To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The most important predictor of a student’s college-going behavior is his or her own academic ability.

(1) the most important predictor of college enrollment is academic preparation; (2) the most important predictors of college completion are academic preparation and financial resources; (3) students with low academic preparation who do enroll in college tend to have low college completion rates; (4) students with low financial resources who have high academic preparation are more likely to complete college than students with high financial resources and low academic preparation; (5) academic preparation and financial support are important for college access and success, and

(1) academic capital formation is a process by which low-income students develop the knowledge, skills, and attitudes that are necessary to succeed in postsecondary education and that (2) academic capital is a resource that can be developed by students and their families and that can be used to improve the college preparation, college access, and college success of low-income students.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which academic capital formation can promote college access and success for low-income students.
the role that academic capital formation plays in the college preparation, college access, and college success of low-income students.
the development of academic capital and the ways it can be used to promote access and success.

the authors provide a conceptual model that explains how low-income students can overcome the barriers to college success.

the book provides a framework to understand the mechanisms that can promote access and success in higher education, and that it offers a set of recommendations for policy makers to consider when developing and implementing policies that can promote the success of low-income students.
the book is a "how to" guide for understanding the complex and interrelated factors that influence the college preparation, admission, and success of students from low-income families.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the current college preparation, access and success of low income youth is not a function of their individual characteristics, but rather a function of the social and cultural capital that their schools, communities, families, and other institutions have provided them.

the college preparation, college access, and college success of low-income students can be enhanced by a combination of three factors: 1) academic capital formation, 2) college knowledge and information, and 3) social capital.
the current system of college access and success is based on a "pipeline" model that is not working well for low-income youth.
